analysis.one_liner: Makes brand-name drug makers pay Medicare-style inflation rebates on drugs sold through private insurance.
analysis.headline: The bill went nowhere: after two committee referrals and two subcommittee referrals over 18 months, it never got a committee vote or floor action, and it died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Current law requires drug makers to pay rebates to Medicare when the prices of brand-name drugs without generics rise faster than inflation — but only on drugs sold through Medicare. This bill would extend that penalty to the same drugs when they're sold through private health insurance, and it would move the starting-year for measuring price increases back from 2021 to 2016, which catches far more price hikes. The result would be direct financial pressure on brand-name manufacturers to stop raising prices faster than inflation on drugs used by the roughly half of Americans with private coverage.
analysis.who_benefits: The tens of millions of Americans who get health insurance through an employer or the private market would benefit indirectly: drug makers facing rebates on every unit sold commercially have a strong reason to slow price increases, which over time would ease premiums and out-of-pocket costs. The Medicare program itself would also collect the rebate payments.

how_it_helps.text: The bill applies the existing Medicare inflation-rebate requirement — covering brand-name drugs costing at least $100 per year with no generic, whose prices rise faster than inflation — to drugs sold in the commercial market under private insurance, with civil penalties for manufacturers that fail to comply.
It also moves the base year used to calculate rebates from 2021 back to 2016, so price increases accumulated over five extra years count against the manufacturer, making the rebate much larger.
The bill excludes units already covered by Medicaid rebates, Part D rebates, and (from 2026) the 340B discount program, so the new rebate targets sales through private insurance specifically.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers would bear the cost, paying inflation-linked rebates to Medicare on drugs they sell into the private market, including rebates calculated retroactively against a 2016 baseline. Insurers and employers might see offsetting pressure on premiums, but the rebate payments themselves come from the manufacturers.

drawbacks.text: The rebates go to the Medicare program, not directly to insured families, so the savings for privately insured people are indirect — felt through slower price growth rather than a visible discount at the pharmacy counter.

The bill makes its changes take effect as if they were part of the original 2022 drug-price law, meaning the 2016 baseline applies retroactively; that would impose a very large one-time rebate liability on manufacturers and is the kind of provision that draws intense industry resistance.

Extending rebates to the entire private market is a far heavier intervention than anything Congress has applied to commercial coverage, and manufacturers and their allies argue that penalties on price increases discourage investment in new medicines — a cost an honest supporter would have to weigh.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside — slowing drug price inflation for everyone with private coverage, at zero direct cost to taxpayers — is substantial, and the bill targets only drugs without generic competition whose prices are rising faster than inflation. The real weaknesses are design and politics: the benefit to families is indirect because the money flows to Medicare, the retroactive 2016 baseline makes the manufacturer burden unusually large and hard to pass, and the industry would fight it hard. It was never actually tested, since no committee ever took it up.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and then a health subcommittee, where it sat for a year and a half without a hearing, markup, or vote, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 14, 2023, and referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees.
On June 16, 2023, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, and it was referred to that subcommittee again on December 17, 2024 — the last action of its life.
The bill never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or a hearing, and it died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill would have extended Medicare's drug inflation rebates to the private insurance market and moved the rebate base year back to 2016, per the CRS summary and bill text.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: they avoided paying inflation rebates on the entire private-insurance market and never faced the retroactive 2016 baseline, and the bill's small pool of sponsors produced no follow-up in the next Congress recorded in these sources.

for.name: Rep. Ruben Gallego
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and pressed for it through subcommittee referral; it received no further action.

for.name: Rep. Elissa Slotkin
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as its only named cosponsor at introduction.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Republican did.

against.role: Referral committee; controlled the Health Subcommittee where the bill sat
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill across 18 months, including a second subcommittee referral in December 2024.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Joint referral committee with jurisdiction over the Medicare provisions
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or any action on the bill before the Congress ended.

against.name: Brand-name drug manufacturers
against.role: Industry that would owe the new rebates
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against expanding the Medicare inflation-rebate program to the commercial market, the drug industry's consistent position on such extensions.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic — the sponsor and two Democratic cosponsors out of 216 House Democrats — with no Republican cosponsors, and the bill's referral committees were under Republican control and never acted on it.

industries.note: They would owe Medicare inflation-linked rebates on every unit of a rebatable drug sold through private insurance, calculated back to a 2016 baseline — a multi-billion-dollar revenue hit. Their interest in blocking the bill ran directly against families facing rising drug prices.

industries.industry: Health insurers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Slower drug price inflation would lower their drug spending and premium pressure, but manufacturers facing new rebates could negotiate harder over plan prices, and the bill does not directly regulate how insurers pass savings to enrollees.
